note: English overlay for content.json. Every field is optional — anything missing falls back to the Vietnamese source. Topics are keyed by their `n`, sections by index. Item translations go under a topic's `items` map, keyed by item id: "items": { "1.1": { "q": "...", "a": "..." } }.

1.label: Java Core & JVM
1.title: Java Core & JVM internals
1.intro: The ground every senior Java backend stands on: memory model, GC, concurrency, and how the JVM actually executes code. This is where your depth shows — build on the recent concurrency deep-dive.

2.label: Java 8→25 & Java vs Go
2.title: Java 8 → 25 (LTS) evolution & Java vs Go
2.intro: A senior should be able to tell the story of where the language went over ten years, and place Java against Go as of 2025–2026, now that both have converged on lightweight concurrency.

3.label: Spring Boot deep dive + build
3.title: Spring & Spring Boot in depth + Maven/Gradle
3.intro: Your daily bread, but at the mechanism level: IoC, transactions, auto-configuration, and managing dependencies properly in the pom/gradle — where framework users part ways with people who understand the framework.

4.label: REST/gRPC & WebFlux
4.title: API protocols (REST/gRPC) & reactive programming (WebFlux)
4.intro: How services talk to each other and handle I/O at a high level. The focus: picking the right protocol, reactive versus virtual threads, and designing a clean API.

5.label: DB core: indexes & locking
5.title: Database core — index internals, transactions, locking
5.intro: Database day one. Down to the algorithm behind an index and the mechanics of InnoDB. The goal: explain what an index is and why it is fast all the way down to the data structure, and read an execution plan fluently.

6.label: DB scaling
6.title: Database scaling — replication, sharding, partitioning
6.intro: Database day two. From one node to many: replicate for reads, shard for writes, and the consistency trade-offs in between. Builds on your AWS RDS experience.

7.label: SQL/NoSQL & DB engines
7.title: SQL vs NoSQL — Oracle / MySQL / PostgreSQL / MongoDB
7.intro: The whole database landscape: when SQL and when NoSQL, why enterprises stay on Oracle, where MySQL and Postgres sit, and why MongoDB reads fast — compared from the software layer down to the physical one.

8.label: Message queue
8.title: Message queue — RabbitMQ vs Kafka
8.intro: The backbone of an event-driven system. Builds on your RabbitMQ Publisher Confirms background and extends into Kafka, so you hold both schools: broker queue versus distributed log.

9.label: Distributed tx (fintech)
9.title: Transactions across services (fintech)
9.intro: What the job description leans on hardest: integration between systems. Keeping money correct as it crosses several services with no global transaction — where real seniority shows in fintech.

10.label: System design + rate limit
10.title: System design foundations, high load & rate limiting
10.intro: The thinking framework, plus the building blocks you assemble a load-bearing system from. Goes deep on the rate-limiting algorithms the job description asks for, and on what it takes to survive high load.

11.label: System design cases
11.title: System design — real interview prompts
11.intro: The framework and the building blocks applied to the classic prompts. Each one lists the requirements, the components, the consistency points and the trade-offs worth saying out loud. Practise the big ones on a 40–45 minute timer.

12.label: Architecture & patterns
12.title: Software architecture: DDD, Clean, Hexagonal & design patterns
12.intro: At the eight-year mark, architecture is the core of what you sell. Know DDD and the dependencies-point-inward architectures, compare them honestly against layered, and reach for patterns where they fit rather than reciting them.
sections: Clean & layered — building it for real

13.label: Security & OAuth2
13.title: Security: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT & designing an auth system
13.intro: Auth is the part you cannot get wrong in fintech. Know OAuth2/OIDC, how a JWT is built and verified, and how to design authentication and authorisation across micro-services.

14.label: DevOps · K8s · best practices
14.title: DevOps & infrastructure: Docker, K8s, Nginx, logging + 2026 best practices
14.intro: Closing the track with production operations: containers, orchestration, web servers, observability at scale, and the industry practices that actually changed recently.

15.label: Network & I/O models
15.title: Networking, protocols & I/O models
15.intro: The network layer and how a server handles concurrency — routinely underrated, and routinely used to test real depth. HTTP/1 through 3, TLS, REST, realtime, and especially how Spring Boot creates and schedules threads, and how event-driven differs from ordinary sequential code.

16.label: Project · concurrency · whiteboard
16.title: The OTA/booking project, concurrency–realtime problems & whiteboard
16.intro: The most hands-on part: presenting and drawing the OTA flight-booking system, the concurrency and realtime problems specific to it, how to tell the most-challenging-project story, and whiteboard practice (design a rate limiter, plus DSA with edge cases).

17.label: REST API design
17.title: REST API design — resources, contracts and lifecycle
17.intro: Topic 4 covers what REST is; this one covers how you design it. From modelling resources and mapping business actions, through idempotency and error standards, to retiring a version without breaking clients — exactly what an interviewer digs into once you say you design APIs.

18.label: Query optimisation
18.title: Query optimisation — read the plan, rewrite it, keep it fast
18.intro: Topic 5 stops at reading EXPLAIN and a handful of techniques. This one walks the whole process: what to measure, how to read a plan, how the optimiser picks a join and when it picks wrong, how to write predicates an index can actually use, and why a fast query suddenly crawls at 2am.
sections: Measure first — reading the execution plan
Rewriting the query & reshaping the model

19.label: DSA & LeetCode
19.title: DSA & LeetCode — the patterns and how to present them
19.intro: A senior backend coding round rarely asks something exotic; it asks something familiar and watches how you present it. This collects the recurring patterns plus the script for thinking out loud — including the one Rakuten actually asked (LC 30).
sections: The patterns that keep coming up

20.label: Observability & SRE
20.title: Observability & SRE — measuring, alerting and handling incidents
20.intro: Topic 14 stops at having logs and metrics. This is the part seniors get dug into: how the three pillars actually differ, how a trace crosses services and queues, what SLOs and error budgets are for, and how to keep alerting from becoming noise everyone mutes.
sections: The three pillars & how to measure

21.label: Linux & production debug
21.title: Linux & production troubleshooting — diagnosing while it burns
21.intro: What separates someone who read the docs from someone who has been on call. Which command you type first when a server crawls, what load average is really telling you, what running out of file descriptors looks like, and how to read a thread dump, heap dump or profile of a live production JVM without making things worse.

22.label: Low-level design / OOD
22.title: Low-level design — designing the classes and writing the code
22.intro: The LLD round sits between DSA and system design: no hard algorithms, no architecture in the clouds — just split the classes and write working code in 45 minutes. Rakuten, Grab, Agoda and most Japanese and global companies run this round.

23.label: Java concurrency coding
23.title: Java concurrency coding — synchronisation problems, written out
23.intro: Topic 1 covers JMM theory and 16.8 names the problems; this is the part you have to type on the board. Bounded queue, interleaved printing, dining philosophers, CAS, CompletableFuture and virtual threads — exactly what gets asked once your CV says strong on concurrency.

24.label: Domain-Driven Design
24.title: Domain-Driven Design — splitting the domain and modelling it
24.intro: Topic 12 introduces DDD in four items; this is what gets dug into once you say you follow DDD. How to find context boundaries, how big an aggregate should be, how a domain event differs from an integration event — and most importantly, when not to use any of it.

micro.title: Microservices at Scale — Technical Mastery Track
micro.intro: The ten problem areas that bite hardest once a system reaches millions of requests, tailored to fintech and airline booking. Every question has a main answer plus a senior deep-dive block.
chapters: 10 · System Design — Putting It All Together
